commenti.body:
I think the answer lies in the fact that it *was* the Writer who said it, rather than anyone else. Writers need to have a good understanding of human nature, so it makes sense that he was the one who deduced the truth. He was also the most cynical of the three. The Stalker was too engrossed in the Zone, the Professor was busy thinking about his professional pride (the phonecall) and blowing up the room. 

I think the Stalker *did* know the truth about the room, but it's hard to say. In the book the film was based on, Roadside Picnic, the Stalker character definitely knows. The book is incredible by the way, well worth a read.

It's not really an absolute truth. It's a theory, albeit a very convincing one that the Writer made after hearing the Porcupine story. He did this in order to convince the Stalker that he wasn't helping anyone. The Stalker is left in an existential crisis by it, and by the Writer asking him if he had ever helped anyone with the Wish Granter. But THB, given how much of the Writer's theory is rooted in your beliefs about the human psyche, you can choose how much you believe it.

Been a long long while since I saw the movie. But I will say that the book, which someone else has mentioned, is less cryptic -- like, less *metaphysically* cryptic? It might fill in some of the gaps for you. (It's also excellent -- I love the Strugatskys)

My sense was that something was going to give with the Stalker's willful ignorance. He wants to give some messianic structure to Porcupine's role. Otherwise, the cause-and-effect of 'Seek brother's life, receive money instead, kill myself' would obliterate his sense of faith.

The Writer, to me, seemed like someone who isn't really capable of controlling when or where his insight hits. He *is* quite observant and his diatribe outside the Room really underlines how obtuse the Stalker and Professor have been acting, but ultimately I think he just 'figured out' the Porcupine thing based on the Stalker's behavior.

Not only does the Stalker *not* know if experiencing the Room is a good thing, he *can't let himself know*. The act of bringing people to the Room is a religious exaltation that the Stalker needs, but at the same time, he truly doesn't want insight into Porpupine's actions (even though, as the Writer points out, the Stalker *does* know.)

To me, it's not so much that the Writer "knows" the reality of the room, it's more like the Stalker has been using 'the Zone' as a physical manifestation of his own issues with faith. Needing it as motivation but lamenting the way it frames his whole life in existential panic. The Writer's gift of emotional/psychological insight allowed him to filter out the abstract metaphysical 'rules' of the Zone from the Stalker's emotionally stunted internal narrative. So his contrarian nature actually helped him in the end, because he realized he couldn't engage with the Room without getting wrapped up in someone else's psychodrama and that would be bad.
